en.title: How the B-21 Raider compares to the B-2 Spirit, B-52 and B-1B — and why it wins every category
en.summary: The B-21 Raider was designed to solve the legacy bomber force's limits on age, survivability and upgrade cost, combining multi-spectral stealth, an open software-defined architecture and a planned fleet of at least 100 aircraft.
body: The United States Air Force has flown the same three bomber platforms for decades: the Boeing B-52H Stratofortress, the Rockwell B-1 Lancer and the Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit. Each has proved its relevance in recent operations, but each also carries a hard ceiling defined by structural age, survivability against peer-level threats, or an architecture that has become prohibitively expensive to upgrade. The Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider was designed to have no equivalent ceiling, and it is the Air Force's answer to all three problems at once.

Against the B-2, the generational gap is architectural as much as physical. The B-2 spans 172 feet (52.4 meters), is 69 feet (21 meters) long, carries up to 40,000 lb (18,144 kg) of ordnance across two internal weapon bays, and flies on four General Electric F118-GE-100 turbofans, each producing 17,300 lb of thrust, with an unrefueled range exceeding 6,000 nautical miles (11,112 km). The B-21 is estimated to be smaller than the B-2, with its precise dimensions still classified, and carries a publicly stated unclassified payload of 30,000 lb (13,608 kg). The B-2's weakness has been maintainability: it reportedly requires as many as 60 maintenance hours per flight hour, and its radar-absorbing coatings demand climate-controlled hangars that exist only at Whiteman Air Force Base and a handful of overseas locations. The B-21 is designed to operate from standard environmental shelters and to accept new weapons, sensors and network integrations as software updates through its open, software-defined mission systems backbone.

The B-1B carries up to 75,000 lb (34,019 kg) of internal ordnance across three internal weapon bays, the largest internal conventional load of any aircraft in the US inventory, and can reach Mach 1.25 on four General Electric F101-GE-102 turbofans, with an unrefueled range exceeding 5,765 nautical miles (10,700 km). More than 40 B-1Bs remain in service, but the Air Force's Bomber Vector plan calls for a phased retirement beginning in FY2028, with the type fully retired by the early 2030s. The B-52J, by contrast, is complementary rather than competitive: replacing its eight Pratt & Whitney TF33 engines with eight Rolls-Royce F130 turbofans, adding a new radar and modernizing communications and navigation, is expected to deliver 30% better fuel efficiency and keep all 76 Stratofortresses flying well past 2050, with initial operational capability targeted for 2033. The B-52J will never penetrate defended airspace; that is the B-21's exclusive domain, operating inside the threat envelope while the B-52J operates outside it.

Scale may be the most strategically significant difference. The Air Force's confirmed procurement target is at least 100 B-21s, with planning discussions of a 145-aircraft fleet, and in February 2026 the Air Force and Northrop Grumman signed a $4.5 billion agreement to increase production capacity by a further 25%. At 100 aircraft the fleet would already be more than five times larger than the 19 operational B-2s; at 145, more than sevenfold. The B-21's flyaway unit cost is targeted at approximately $700 million, roughly a third of what each B-2 costs when development expenditure is spread across the fleet. The first operational B-21 is expected to arrive at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027.

The B-2 reportedly requires as many as 60 maintenance hours per flight hour and climate-controlled hangars, whereas the B-21 is designed to operate from standard environmental shelters with an open, software-defined mission systems backbone.

More than 40 B-1Bs remain in service, with a phased retirement planned from FY2028 and full retirement by the early 2030s; the B-52J re-engining is expected to deliver 30% better fuel efficiency and keep 76 Stratofortresses flying well past 2050.

zh.title: B-21對比B-2、B-52與B-1B：隱形、架構與規模決定下一代轟炸機主力
zh.summary: B-21突襲者的設計目標，是同時解決舊型轟炸機隊的老化、面對同級威脅的存活能力與升級成本過高三個問題，並以至少100架的規劃機隊成為美國空軍未來的全球打擊主力。
body: 美國空軍數十年來使用同一批三款轟炸機：波音B-52H同溫層堡壘、洛克威爾B-1槍騎兵與諾斯洛普格魯曼B-2幽靈。每款都在近年的作戰中證明過價值，但也各有難以突破的上限：結構老化、面對同級威脅的存活能力，或是升級成本已經高到難以負擔。諾斯洛普格魯曼B-21突襲者的設計目標就是沒有同等的上限，要一次解決這三個問題。

與B-2相比，世代差距不只在外形，更在架構。B-2翼展172英尺（52.4公尺）、機長69英尺（21公尺），兩個內部彈艙可攜帶最多40,000磅（18,144公斤）彈藥，使用4具奇異F118-GE-100渦扇發動機，每具推力17,300磅，不加油航程超過6,000海里（11,112公里）。B-21據估計比B-2小，精確尺寸仍屬機密，公開的非機密載彈量為30,000磅（13,608公斤）。B-2真正的弱點是維護：據報導每飛行小時需要最多60小時維護，雷達吸波塗層還需要恆溫恆濕機庫，而這類機庫只有懷特曼空軍基地與少數海外地點才有。B-21則設計為可在一般環境掩體中操作，並透過開放式軟體定義任務系統架構，把新武器、感測器與網路整合當成軟體更新推送。

B-1B的三個內部彈艙可攜帶最多75,000磅（34,019公斤）內部彈藥，是美國軍機中最大的內部傳統彈藥酬載，使用4具奇異F101-GE-102渦扇發動機，最高速度1.25馬赫，不加油航程超過5,765海里（10,700公里）。目前仍有40多架B-1B在役，但空軍的轟炸機計畫要求自2028財政年度起分階段退役，2030年代初全數退役。B-52J則不是競爭對手，而是互補角色：把8具普惠TF33發動機換成8具勞斯萊斯F130渦扇發動機、換裝新雷達並更新通訊與導航設備後，預計燃油效率提升30%，76架同溫層堡壘可飛到2050年代以後，初始作戰能力目標為2033年。B-52J永遠無法穿透防禦空域，那是B-21的專屬領域：B-52J在威脅範圍外作戰，B-21則深入其中。
規模可能是最具戰略意義的差異。空軍已確認的B-21採購目標至少100架，規劃討論中還出現145架的數字；2026年2月，空軍與諾斯洛普格魯曼簽署45億美元協議，把產能再提升25%。100架的機隊已是19架現役B-2的5倍以上，145架則是7倍以上。B-21單機飛離價格目標約7億美元，大約是攤提研發成本後每架B-2成本的三分之一。首架作戰型B-21預計2027年進駐南達科他州艾爾斯渥斯空軍基地。
